analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from January 2023 until the Congress ended, with no committee vote, no floor vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar sitting members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, options, commodities, and similar investments while in office. It allows widely diversified mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and Treasury securities, and holdings in a qualified blind trust. Members who violate the ban would have to hand over any profits to the Treasury, could face civil fines from the ethics committees, and could not deduct related losses on their taxes. Each member would certify compliance annually, and the Government Accountability Office would audit compliance within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who cannot act on nonpublic information they may encounter at work. By removing the ability of lawmakers to trade individual stocks while writing laws and overseeing the companies affected, the bill aims to eliminate a conflict of interest between members' personal portfolios and the public interest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and citizens without insider access

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding, purchasing, or selling individual securities, commodities, derivatives, and comparable synthetic interests during their term of service, allowing only diversified funds and Treasury securities.

Requires members to disgorge any profit from a violating trade to the Treasury, subjects violators to civil fines assessed by the ethics committees, and bars deducting losses from violating trades on income taxes.

Requires an annual written certification of compliance from every member, published on a public website, and directs the Comptroller General to audit members' compliance and report results within two years.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stocks within 180 days or place them in a blind trust, giving up a source of personal investment returns that is open to most other high-income households.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement design leaves the fox guarding the henhouse in places: fines are assessed by the Senate and House ethics committees, whose members are sitting legislators, and a member fined can appeal by privileged motion to a vote of the full chamber where their party colleagues sit.

The ban excludes diversified mutual funds and ETFs, so members could still hold broad market positions in companies they regulate; it targets company-specific trading, not all exposure to markets they influence.

Members could shift company-specific holdings into a qualified blind trust, which reduces but does not eliminate the appearance of conflict, since a trustee could still be aware of the member's identity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is institutional: removing a real conflict of interest in which lawmakers can trade on information from their work and vote on matters affecting their own portfolios. The cost falls almost entirely on the roughly 535 people who would have to divest, a cost the public generally bears little sympathy for. The main weakness is enforcement, since ethics committees made of the members' own colleagues assess the fines.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hawley introduced the bill on January 24, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action ever occurred: the Finance Committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it.
The bill drew no cosponsors at any point in the two-year Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed die when a Congress ends; S. 58 was not reintroduced in this record and lapsed with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress who own or trade individual stocks are better off: they kept the ability to trade securities while in office, subject only to the existing disclosure rules, because the ban was never enacted.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it after the former House Speaker to draw attention to congressional stock trading; did not attract any cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the entire two-year Congress, never holding a markup or voting to report it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call to examine; the only sponsorship was a single Republican senator with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Sitting members of Congress who hold or trade individual securities
industries.note: By failing to act, Congress kept in place the ability of its own members to buy and sell individual stocks, options, and commodities while voting on and overseeing the same companies. The bill would have required divestment, profit disgorgement, and audits; its death preserved the status quo for the one group it targeted.
